section.title: The Sermon on the Mount: Prayer and Treasure
section.sectionRationale: The Sermon turns from outward conduct to the hidden life before God. Jesus warns against practicing giving, prayer, and fasting to be seen by others, gives the model prayer, and then calls His people to a single-hearted devotion that stores treasure in heaven, serves God rather than money, and trusts the Father instead of being consumed by worry.
section.thesis: True righteousness is lived before the Father who sees in secret, not staged for human applause, and it flows from a heart set on God alone, so that His people pray to their Father, treasure heaven above earth, serve God rather than money, and are freed from anxiety to seek first His kingdom.
section.frameNote: Seven beats: giving in secret; prayer without hypocrisy; the model prayer; forgiveness; secret fasting; treasure in heaven and undivided service; and freedom from worry through trust in the Father.

units.label: Giving in secret
units.note: your Father who sees in secret

verses.text: “Be careful not to perform your righteous acts before men to be seen by them. If you do, you will have no reward from your Father in heaven.

So when you give to the needy, do not sound a trumpet before you, as the {{hypokrites|hypocrites}} do in the synagogues and on the streets, to be honored by men. Truly I tell you, they already have their full reward.
But when you give to the needy, do not let your left hand know what your right hand is doing,
so that your giving may be in secret. And your Father, who sees what is done in secret, will reward you.

units.label: How to pray
units.note: your Father knows what you need

verses.text: And when you pray, do not be like the hypocrites. For they love to pray standing in the synagogues and on the street corners to be seen by men. Truly I tell you, they already have their full reward.
But when you pray, go into your inner room, shut your door, and pray to your Father, who is unseen. And your Father, who sees what is done in secret, will reward you.
And when you pray, do not babble on like pagans, for they think that by their many words they will be heard.
Do not be like them, for your Father knows what you need before you ask Him.
So then, this is how you should pray: ‘Our Father in heaven, hallowed be Your name.
Your kingdom come, Your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven.
Give us this day our {{epiousios|daily}} bread.
And forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors.
And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from the evil one.’
For if you forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you.
But if you do not forgive men their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive yours.
When you fast, do not be somber like the hypocrites, for they disfigure their faces to show men they are fasting. Truly I tell you, they already have their full reward.
But when you fast, anoint your head and wash your face,
so that your fasting will not be obvious to men, but only to your Father, who is unseen. And your Father, who sees what is done in secret, will reward you.

units.label: Treasure and the single eye
units.note: you cannot serve God and money

verses.text: Do not store up for yourselves treasures on earth, where moth and rust destroy, and where thieves break in and steal.
But store up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where moth and rust do not destroy, and where thieves do not break in and steal.
For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.
The eye is the lamp of the body. If your eyes are good, your whole body will be full of light.
But if your eyes are bad, your whole body will be full of darkness. If then the light within you is darkness, how great is that darkness!
No one can serve two masters: Either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will be devoted to the one and despise the other. You cannot serve both God and {{mamonas|money}}.
Therefore I tell you, do not {{merimnao|worry}} about your life, what you will eat or drink; or about your body, what you will wear. Is not life more than food, and the body more than clothes?
Look at the birds of the air: They do not sow or reap or gather into barns, and yet your heavenly Father feeds them. Are you not much more valuable than they?
Who of you by worrying can add a single hour to his life?
And why do you worry about clothes? Consider how the lilies of the field grow: They do not labor or spin.
Yet I tell you that not even Solomon in all his glory was adorned like one of these.
If that is how God clothes the grass of the field, which is here today and tomorrow is thrown into the furnace, will He not much more clothe you, O you of little faith?
Therefore do not worry, saying, ‘What shall we eat?’ or ‘What shall we drink?’ or ‘What shall we wear?’
For the Gentiles strive after all these things, and your heavenly Father knows that you need them.
But seek first the kingdom of God and His righteousness, and all these things will be added unto you.
Therefore do not worry about tomorrow, for tomorrow will worry about itself. Today has enough trouble of its own.

hypokrites.gloss: Hypocrite, originally an actor who plays a part behind a mask. Jesus uses it for those who perform their religion for an audience of people rather than God; they win human applause and forfeit the Father's reward.

epiousios.gloss: A rare word rendered daily, likely meaning the bread needed for the coming day. It teaches dependence on the Father for each day's provision, echoing Israel's daily manna in the wilderness.

mamonas.gloss: Mammon, wealth or money personified as a rival master. Jesus presents money as a would-be lord that competes with God for the heart's allegiance; one cannot be a slave to both.

merimnao.gloss: To be anxious, worried, pulled apart by care. Jesus repeatedly forbids this corroding worry over food and clothing, calling His people instead to trust the Father's provision and seek first His kingdom.

basic.context: Jesus moves from how we treat others to the hidden life of devotion. He warns that giving, praying, and fasting done to impress people get only the reward of being noticed. Instead, do them before the Father who sees in secret. He gives the model prayer, teaches that we must forgive to be forgiven, and then calls for a single-hearted life: store treasure in heaven, serve God not money, and stop worrying, because the Father feeds the birds and clothes the lilies.
basic.hermeneutics: Read the first half as a critique of religion performed for an audience, with the refrain your Father who sees in secret. Read the Lord's Prayer as a pattern to shape all our praying, not just words to recite. The second half exposes the heart's true master: what we treasure, whom we serve, and what we worry about all reveal where our trust really lies.
basic.originalLanguages: The hypocrites are play-actors, performing religion for applause. In the prayer we ask for daily bread, the provision needed for each coming day, like manna. Jesus names money as a rival master, mammon, that competes with God for our hearts. And He forbids the corroding worry that pulls us apart, calling us to trust the Father instead.
basic.typology: The daily bread echoes the manna God gave Israel each morning in the wilderness, teaching daily dependence. The Father who clothes the lilies and feeds the birds is the Creator of Genesis, still sustaining His world. And the treasure in heaven points to the inheritance kept for God's people that no thief can touch.
basic.christ: Jesus teaches us to call God our Father, a intimacy grounded in His own Sonship, into which He brings us. He is the one whose whole life was lived before the Father, not for human applause. He is the treasure worth more than all the world, and the one who models perfect trust in the Father's care, even to the cross.
basic.god: The Father is the great theme: He sees in secret and rewards, He knows our needs before we ask, He feeds the birds and clothes the grass, and He is worthy of undivided service. He is a Father to be trusted, not a distant power to be manipulated with many words or impressed with public displays.
basic.crossReferences: Exodus 16 gives the daily manna behind daily bread. Luke 11 has a parallel form of the Lord's Prayer. 1 Timothy 6 warns that the love of money is a root of evil. And 1 Peter 5 urges us to cast our anxiety on God because He cares.
basic.oneStory: The King calls His people to live the whole of life before the face of their Father. Religion becomes real when it is done for God's eyes, not the crowd's; prayer becomes intimate when addressed to a Father who already knows our needs; and life becomes free when the heart treasures God above money and trusts Him for daily bread. All of it flows from knowing God as Father, the relationship Jesus came to open.

context.literary:
Matthew 6 is the middle chapter of the Sermon on the Mount, and it has two halves with a clear hinge. The first half, verses 1 to 18, deals with three acts of devotion, giving, prayer and fasting, in a repeated pattern: 'when you' do the act, do not do it like the hypocrites, they have their reward already, but do it in secret and 'your Father, who sees what is done in secret, will reward you.' That refrain appears in verses 4, 6 and 18, and the opening warning of verse 1 states the principle for all three. The prayer section is expanded with a comment on empty words, verses 7 and 8, the model prayer, verses 9 to 13, and a comment on forgiveness, verses 14 and 15. Many readers notice that the central act, prayer, receives the most space.

The second half, verses 19 to 34, turns from devotion to possessions and anxiety. It runs through three paired contrasts: treasure on earth or in heaven, a sound eye or a bad eye, God or money. It closes with the long command not to worry, which repeats the question 'what shall we eat?' and rounds on the answer that the Father knows. The lines 'where your treasure is, there your heart will be also,' verse 21, and 'seek first the kingdom,' verse 33, are the two summits.

The Lord's Prayer is itself built in two parts. The first three petitions concern the Father, 'Your name, Your kingdom, Your will,' and the last three concern us, 'give us, forgive us, lead us.' The order matters: God's glory is placed before our needs.

The chapter keeps returning to a few terms, 'Father,' 'reward,' 'see,' 'treasure' and 'heart.' Together they say that the whole of life is lived before the Father's eyes, and that what a person treasures shows where the heart rests.
context.historical:
The three acts of the first half, almsgiving, prayer and fasting, were the usual signs of devotion in Jewish life, and Jesus assumes His hearers will do them: He says 'when you give,' 'when you pray,' 'when you fast,' not 'if.' Because they were visible signs of piety, they were also open to display. Prayer in the synagogue and on the street corner was not wrong in itself, since there were appointed hours of prayer, such as the ninth hour, Acts 3:1, and public places where people stopped to pray. The danger was staging it. Fasting was practised by the devout, and a Pharisee in one of Jesus' parables boasts, 'I fast twice a week,' Luke 18:12. The 'trumpet' in verse 2 is probably a figure for drawing attention, since we have no clear evidence that people literally blew horns when giving.

In the Roman-ruled Galilee most people lived close to the margin. Bread was the staple, and a day's wage bought a day's food, so the petition for bread for today was a daily reality for many. Wealth was stored in clothing, grain and coin, and clothes were a real form of savings, which is why moths were a threat to wealth, Job 13:28 and James 5:2. The verb in verse 19 for thieves who 'break in' literally means to dig through, since many houses had walls of mud brick.

The word 'Gentiles' in verses 7 and 32 recalls the pagan world, where prayer often meant lengthy strings of names and formulas meant to gain the attention of a god. Solomon, whom Jesus names in verse 29, was the image of Israelite wealth and splendour, 1 Kings 10:4-7. The Galilean hillside offered wild flowers and birds in view, and Jesus uses what His audience could see.
context.canonical:
The chapter belongs to the Old Testament's picture of God as Father and as the one who sees. Israel was God's son, Exodus 4:22, and the prophets could say, 'You, O LORD, are our Father,' Isaiah 63:16. A psalm says, 'As a father has compassion on his children, so the LORD has compassion on those who fear Him,' Psalm 103:13. Hagar named God 'the God who sees me,' Genesis 16:13, and Psalm 139:1-4 says He knows our words before they are spoken, which is exactly the point of Matthew 6:8.

The petitions of the Lord's Prayer have roots in the prophets. God says He will show the holiness of His great name, Ezekiel 36:23, which stands behind 'hallowed be Your name.' The kingdom is the one given to the Son of Man in Daniel 7:13-14. The request for daily bread recalls the manna, when God told Moses that the people were to gather 'enough for that day,' Exodus 16:4, and the wise man's prayer, 'feed me with the bread that is my portion,' Proverbs 30:8. Jesus Himself prays 'may Your will be done' in Gethsemane, Matthew 26:42, and later teaches that those who enter the kingdom do 'the will of My Father in heaven,' Matthew 7:21.

Luke records a shorter form of the prayer in Luke 11:2-4, and the early church treasured it; the Didache, a first or second century Christian manual, tells believers to pray it three times a day. Paul says that the Spirit teaches believers to cry 'Abba, Father,' Romans 8:15 and Galatians 4:6.

The teaching on treasure and worry is echoed in many places. Luke has parallels in Luke 12:22-34 and 16:13, Paul says 'the love of money is the root of all kinds of evil,' 1 Timothy 6:10, and Hebrews tells us to be free from the love of money because God has said, 'Never will I leave you,' Hebrews 13:5. Peter and Paul both say, in different words, that we may cast our anxiety on God, 1 Peter 5:7 and Philippians 4:6-7, following Psalm 55:22.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Matthew's aim in this chapter is to shift his readers' attention from the audience in front of them to the Father above them. The earlier part of the sermon has shown what righteousness looks like in conduct; chapter 6 asks whom it is for. Jesus is not telling His people to hide their devotion for its own sake. He is warning against devotion that is performed for approval, a mistake that those who were most religious were most likely to make. Behind every instruction lies a single question: before whose eyes do you live?

The chapter also aims to teach prayer as a relationship. Jesus sets the Father who knows what we need against the pagan idea that gods must be persuaded. Because prayer is addressed to a Father, it can be simple, and because He is in heaven, it begins with His name and kingdom. The prayer's concern for daily bread, forgiveness and rescue shows that no area of life is outside it.

Finally, the second half tries to free people from the two great rivals of the Father's rule, money and worry. These are not only temptations of the rich; the worry passage is addressed to people who are anxious about food and clothes, and so to the poor. Jesus' answer is not a technique for calming down but a reason to trust: the Father who feeds the birds knows our needs and has made His kingdom the first priority.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Most of this chapter is direct instruction in the imperative: do not perform your righteous acts to be seen, pray like this, forgive, do not store up treasure on earth, do not worry. These are meant to be obeyed. Yet some details are vivid pictures, not literal rules, and they ask to be read for their point. The left hand not knowing what the right is doing, verse 3, is an idiom for giving without self-congratulation, and it does not forbid keeping accounts or giving through a church. The command to shut the door and pray in the inner room does not forbid public or corporate prayer, since Jesus Himself prayed with others and taught a prayer in the plural, 'Our Father.' The target is prayer made to be seen.

The Lord's Prayer is introduced with 'this is how you should pray,' which makes it a pattern. The church has used it as words to say together, and that is a fair use; but Jesus' emphasis falls on the shape, the priority of the Father's name and kingdom, then our bread, forgiveness and protection. The command not to worry is not a command to be careless, since the same Gospel commends work and planning elsewhere; it forbids the kind of anxiety that makes a person a slave to provision. The promise that 'all these things will be added' is a promise about the Father's care, not a guarantee that no believer will ever go hungry.

debates.question: What does daily bread mean in the Lord's Prayer?

views.label: The provision needed for each day
views.case: The rare word most naturally means the bread necessary for the coming day, teaching daily dependence on the Father, echoing the manna Israel gathered each morning.

views.label: A richer, forward-looking bread
views.case: Some see an echo of the bread of the age to come or the sustaining grace of God's kingdom, so that the petition reaches beyond mere food to God's full provision for His people.

debates.bearing: Either way the petition teaches humble, daily reliance on the Father for all we need, body and soul, rather than anxious self-sufficiency.

debates.question: Does our forgiving others earn God's forgiveness?

views.label: Forgiving is the evidence, not the cause, of being forgiven
views.case: Those truly forgiven by God become forgiving; a persistently unforgiving heart shows it has never grasped grace, so Jesus warns that such a person is not in fact reconciled to God.

views.label: A real, covenantal condition of ongoing fellowship
views.case: Jesus states a genuine link: the Father withholds forgiveness from the unforgiving, not because grace is earned, but because refusing to forgive others is incompatible with living under His mercy.

debates.bearing: Both agree that a settled refusal to forgive cannot coexist with receiving God's forgiveness; grace received always overflows in grace given.

debates.question: What does 'lead us not into temptation' ask, given that God tempts no one?

views.label: Spare us from trials that might overcome us
views.case: The Greek word peirasmos covers both testing and temptation, and Jesus Himself was 'led' into a trial in Matthew 4:1. The petition asks the Father not to bring His children into a testing they could not bear, and to keep them from falling in it.

views.label: A request to be kept from sin in the trial
views.case: Since James says God 'tempts no one,' James 1:13, the prayer asks that we not be allowed to fall into the snare of the tempter. The second half, 'deliver us from the evil one,' then explains the first, asking for rescue from the enemy.

views.label: A prayer about the final great trial
views.case: Some read the petition in the light of the end of the age, when great testing is expected. It asks to be kept faithful in the last days, which fits Jesus' word to His disciples in Luke 22:40, 'Pray that you will not enter into temptation.'

debates.bearing: Every view agrees that the prayer expresses dependence. We do not trust ourselves in a test, and we ask the Father who is stronger than the evil one to keep us.

study.originalLanguages:
The word 'reward' in the opening warning is misthos, wages, and Jesus says of the hypocrites that 'they already have their full reward.' The verb is apecho, a word that was used in receipts, so that the idea is of a bill marked 'paid in full.' They wanted applause and they got it, and nothing more is owed them. The Father's reward, by contrast, is given by grace, since He gives to the one who asks for nothing.

In verse 6 the 'inner room' is the tameion, the storeroom or small chamber of a house, often the only room that could be closed off. It is a plain, even humble place. The word for 'babble' in verse 7, battalogeo, is a rare word that sounds like empty chatter, and it names the habit of piling up phrases. Jesus does not forbid long prayers, since He spent nights in prayer, but He forbids the notion that the number of words wins a hearing.

The prayer begins 'Our Father in heaven.' In Greek 'heaven' is plural, 'in the heavens,' a Jewish way of speaking of God's dwelling. The first three petitions use the aorist imperative, 'hallowed be,' 'come,' 'be done,' which are urgent requests for a decisive act. The verb 'hallow' means to make holy, to treat as holy, and when it is passive it is a request that God Himself will cause His name to be honoured, as He promises in Ezekiel 36:23.

The word for 'debts' in verse 12 is opheilemata, the ordinary term for what is owed. The parallel in verse 14 uses 'trespasses,' paraptomata, a word for a false step, and Luke's version has 'sins.' All three images, debt, slip and sin, are used for the same thing. In the parable of the unforgiving servant the idea of a debt that cannot be repaid is made vivid, Matthew 18:21-35.

The word 'temptation' in verse 13 is peirasmos, the word for the testing in Matthew 4, and 'the evil one' can also be read 'evil,' as the BSB footnote notes. Many manuscripts end the prayer with 'For Yours is the kingdom and the power and the glory,' but the BSB places this in a footnote, since it is probably a later addition drawn from the church's worship.

The 'eye' passage depends on two words, haplous, 'sound' or 'single,' and poneros, 'bad.' The BSB footnote says the Greek literally reads 'If your eye is sound' and 'if your eye is evil,' pointing to Proverbs 22:9 and Proverbs 28:22. In the Old Testament a generous eye and a stingy eye are ways of speaking about openhandedness, as when the vineyard owner asks, 'are you envious because I am generous?' Matthew 20:15, where the Greek says 'is your eye evil.' So Jesus' words about the eye are about generosity as much as clarity.

In verse 24 'serve' is douleuo, to serve as a slave, so the issue is ownership and not job preference. 'Money' is the Aramaic mamonas. In verse 27 the phrase 'a single hour' can also mean 'a single cubit,' a measure of height, as the footnote says; either way, worry adds nothing. In verse 28 'consider' is a strong verb meaning to learn carefully from something, and in verse 30 'little faith' is a single word, oligopistos, which Jesus uses elsewhere of disciples in a storm, Matthew 8:26. The last verb of verse 33 is passive, 'will be added,' so the one who adds is the Father.

typology.fulfillment: Israel was told to gather bread 'enough for that day,' and what was kept overnight spoiled, Exodus 16:4 and 19-20. The petition 'Give us this day our daily bread' repeats that discipline in prayer. The correspondence grows in Christ, who says, 'I am the bread of life,' John 6:35, so that the bread we pray for is finally the One who gives it. The type falls short in that manna was for the body and for a season, while the bread of life satisfies for ever.

typology.type: The Father who feeds and clothes
typology.fulfillment: The psalmist says that all creatures look to God for their food and that He satisfies them when He opens His hand, Psalm 104:27-28, and that He feeds the young ravens, Psalm 147:9. Jesus draws on this theology of creation and presses the argument: if God feeds birds and clothes grass, He will care for His children. The picture points to the Father's care in Christ, in whom God supplies even more, 'though He was rich, yet for your sakes He became poor,' 2 Corinthians 8:9. The type is limited because creation's care is general, while the care shown in Christ is personal and eternal.

Jesus contrasts treasure that moths and thieves can take with a treasure in heaven. In another parable the kingdom is a hidden treasure for which a man sells all he has, Matthew 13:44. Paul counts everything as loss 'compared to the surpassing excellence of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord,' Philippians 3:8, and says that the believer's life is 'hidden with Christ in God,' Colossians 3:3. The heavenly treasure is therefore a person and a share in His inheritance. The image falls short only because treasure sounds like a thing, while the reward Jesus gives is a relationship.

typology.type: The single eye and the undivided heart
typology.fulfillment: The sound eye of verse 22 recalls the Old Testament call to love the LORD with all the heart, which Jesus calls the first commandment, Matthew 22:37-38, and Proverbs 22:9 speaks of the generous eye. The picture of a whole body full of light looks forward to the new creation, where the people of God see Him, and ahead to Christ, who has a single devotion to the Father: 'not as I will, but as You will,' Matthew 26:39. The type is fulfilled in Him alone, and His people share it by the Spirit.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ first through the word Father. Jesus teaches His disciples to say 'Our Father,' but He says it as the Son, whose relation to the Father is unique. He says elsewhere that He has made the Father's name known, John 17:6, and Paul says that the Spirit of the Son makes believers cry, 'Abba, Father,' Galatians 4:6. The intimacy of the Lord's Prayer is therefore a gift: those who pray share in the Son's own standing. The prayer does not teach us how to approach a distant God; it invites us into a family.

It leads to Christ by His own life. Jesus lived this chapter. He gave, prayed and fasted before the Father and not for the crowd, going off to pray alone, as Matthew 14:23 shows, and He fasted in the wilderness without display. He prayed the prayer's petitions from the heart, 'may Your will be done,' Matthew 26:42, in the garden where His anxiety was greatest and His trust was deepest. He is the one who truly sought first the kingdom and His righteousness.

It leads to Christ through forgiveness. The prayer asks the Father to forgive our debts as we forgive, and the way that forgiveness is possible is the cross. Paul says, 'forgiving each other just as in Christ God forgave you,' Ephesians 4:32. The pattern is that grace received overflows in grace given. Jesus' own prayer on the cross, 'Father, forgive them,' Luke 23:34, is the prayer of this chapter said in the worst situation.

It leads to Christ through treasure. Jesus is the one who 'though He was rich, yet for your sakes He became poor,' 2 Corinthians 8:9. He is also the treasure that is worth everything, the pearl and the field in the parables. When He says the heart follows the treasure, He offers Himself as a treasure that cannot be stolen, since He is risen and our life is hidden with Him, Colossians 3:3.

It leads to Christ through the provision of daily bread. He is the Bread of life, John 6:35, and at His table the bread of the age to come is given. Some have heard in the prayer's rare word for 'daily' a hint of the bread of tomorrow's kingdom, though the word is difficult and we should hold that lightly.

A word of caution is needed. This chapter is not a hidden allegory of Christ in every detail; the lilies, the birds and the moth are not secret figures for Him. The links above rest on what the New Testament itself says about the Father and the Son. The chapter's own point is the Father's care, and Christ is the one who brings us to the Father and shows us what that care costs, since He who commands us not to worry was Himself troubled in Gethsemane and trusted anyway.
study.god:
The chapter's central doctrine is the fatherhood of God. The word 'Father' occurs again and again, and each time it carries a different shade: the Father who sees in secret, who knows what we need, who forgives, who feeds the birds, and who knows we need food and clothing. This is not a vague parental kindness; it is a Father with a name to be hallowed, a kingdom to come and a will to be done. His fatherhood is joined with His kingship and His holiness.

It shows a God who sees. The repeated phrase 'who sees what is done in secret' means that nothing is hidden from Him, and that is both a warning and a comfort. It is a warning for those who perform righteousness for show, since the only audience that matters sees through the performance. It is a comfort for those who serve unnoticed, because their giving, praying and fasting are known. Hagar called Him 'the God who sees me,' Genesis 16:13, and Psalm 139 says He knows the word before it is on the tongue.

It shows a God who knows. 'Your Father knows what you need before you ask Him,' verse 8. That seems to make prayer pointless, but Jesus draws the opposite conclusion: because He knows, we do not need to convince Him, and we can pray plainly. Prayer is not information for God but fellowship with Him, in which we put our needs in His hands.

It shows a God who provides. He feeds the birds, clothes the grass and cares for His people. His providence is generous and reliable, and it reaches down to the details of daily bread. God's way of providing is also a way of teaching: manna taught Israel dependence, and the prayer teaches it again.

It shows a God who is jealous for the whole heart. He is not content to share rule with money, 'You cannot serve both God and money.' He claims the whole person, and He alone is worthy of that claim. At the same time He is not a tyrant who hoards our loyalty for His own gain; He is a Father who knows that a divided heart is a harmed heart.

It shows a God who forgives and expects His children to forgive. The link between His forgiveness and ours reflects His character: those who share His mercy cannot be hard toward others.

For worship, the chapter calls us to pray with the confidence of children and the reverence due to a holy name. It asks us to give up the effort to impress, to bring our needs without anxiety, and to keep our eyes on the Father, whose kingdom, power and glory are the final concern of everything.

crossReferences.note: The manna story behind 'daily bread.' God promised bread from heaven, told the people to gather enough for the day, and let leftovers spoil. The petition teaches the same daily dependence, with the Father's faithfulness every morning as its ground.

A wise man prays, 'Give me neither poverty nor riches; feed me with the bread that is my portion.' He fears that too much would make him forget God and too little would tempt him to steal. It is a close parallel to the balance of the Lord's Prayer's request for today's bread.

God promises to show the holiness of His great name before the nations. It stands behind the first petition, 'hallowed be Your name,' which asks that God would Himself act to make His name honoured, as He promises to do when He gives His Spirit and renews His people.

Luke's version of the prayer comes in answer to a disciple's request, 'Lord, teach us to pray,' and is followed by the parable of the persistent friend and the promise that the Father gives the Holy Spirit to those who ask. It shows that the prayer was a repeated teaching, used on more than one occasion.

The parable of the servant forgiven a huge debt who will not forgive a small one. It illustrates verses 14 and 15 by showing what it means to receive mercy and refuse to give it, and why the Father is angered when a forgiven person is unforgiving.

God asks whether a fast of bowed heads and sackcloth is what He chose, and says the fast He wants is to loose chains, share bread with the hungry and clothe the naked. It matches Jesus' concern that fasting not be a display, and that devotion to God be joined with justice.

The BSB footnote points here for the 'sound' eye of Matthew 6:22, which in the Hebrew idiom is the generous eye: 'A generous man will be blessed, for he shares his bread with the poor.' It explains why Jesus connects the eye with money and giving.

Jesus says, 'You cannot serve both God and money,' in nearly the same words, at the end of the parable of the shrewd manager. It shows that the saying was a standing part of His teaching and that it applies to the use of wealth as much as to the attitude toward it.

All creatures look to God for their food, and when He opens His hand they are satisfied. It is the creation theology behind the birds and lilies of verses 26 to 30, and it shows that Jesus' argument 'how much more' is built on Israel's own praise.

Paul teaches that godliness with contentment is great gain, and that the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil. It carries the second half of Matthew 6 into the church's life, applying Jesus' warning about treasure and service to the dangers of wanting to be rich.

Paul writes, 'Be anxious for nothing, but in everything, by prayer and petition, with thanksgiving, present your requests to God.' It is the apostolic echo of Matthew 6:25 to 34: the cure for anxiety is to bring each need to the Father, and the result is a peace that guards the heart.

'Cast all your anxiety on Him, because He cares for you.' Peter was in the circle that heard the sermon, and his instruction takes up its thought and its reason. The ground of the command is not the strength of the one who worries but the care of the one who is addressed.

study.oneStory:
The Bible opens with a world in which God provides richly and people live under His eye, in a garden where every need was supplied and the only command was to trust and obey. The fall began as a loss of that trust: the serpent suggested that God was holding something back, and the man and woman reached for more than they had been given. From that moment, people have been hiding from the Father, striving for their own provision and seeking approval from others. The two great themes of Matthew 6, performance for human eyes and anxiety over provision, are the long-run fruit of that distrust.

Israel's story carries the same pattern. In the wilderness God fed His people with manna, one day at a time, to teach them to trust Him, and they grumbled and hoarded. In the land they were warned against forgetting the LORD when they were full, Proverbs 30:9. The prophets denounced worship that was show without heart, and the Psalms sang of the God who feeds the birds and satisfies every living thing.

Matthew 6 is the Messiah's call back to that trust. He teaches His people to address God as Father, which the Old Testament seldom did so directly, and He bases the invitation on the nearness of His own kingdom. The prayer He gives asks for the coming of that kingdom, for the Father's will to be done on earth as it is in heaven, which is a prayer for the undoing of the fall. The call to seek first the kingdom is a call to reorder life around the reign that is now arriving.

The chapter looks ahead to Gethsemane, where the Son prays the prayer in earnest, and to the cross, where the debt of His people is paid. After that the Spirit teaches believers to cry 'Abba, Father,' Romans 8:15, and the church prays the prayer with the confidence of those who are already sons and daughters.

The story ends with prayers answered. The Father's name will be hallowed and His kingdom will have come, His will will be done on earth as in heaven, and the hunger and debt and temptation of this age will be over. In the new creation 'they will see His face,' Revelation 22:4, and the Father who saw in secret will welcome His children into the open. The treasure stored in heaven will be fully theirs, and worry will have no place, for the Lord God will be their light.

quiz.q: What is Jesus' main warning about giving, prayer, and fasting?

options.text: Do not do them to be seen by others, but before the Father who sees in secret.
options.note: Verses 1-18 repeat this contrast between human applause and the Father's reward.

options.text: Do them privately so that no one is ever helped by your example.
options.note: The aim is sincerity before God, not hiding all good works; Jesus elsewhere says let your light shine. This overstates secrecy.

options.text: Avoid them altogether to escape the temptation of pride.
options.note: Jesus assumes His people will give, pray, and fast; the issue is the audience and motive, not abstaining.

options.text: Perform them publicly to encourage others to do the same.
options.note: The opposite of His warning; doing them to be seen forfeits the Father's reward.

quiz.q: How does Jesus teach His disciples to pray?

options.text: To their Father who knows their needs, using the pattern of the Lord's Prayer.
options.note: Verses 6-13 direct prayer to the Father and give the model prayer.

options.text: With many repeated words to be sure God hears them.
options.note: Jesus rejects this pagan babbling; He wants trusting, simple prayer to the Father who already knows our needs.

options.text: Only in public gatherings at the synagogue.
options.note: He commends private prayer to the Father, not public display, as the primary posture.

options.text: Silently, since God does not want us to ask for anything.
options.note: Jesus tells us to ask, giving a whole prayer of petitions; God invites our requests.

quiz.q: Why should disciples store up treasures in heaven rather than on earth?

options.text: Earthly treasure perishes, and where your treasure is, your heart will be also.
options.note: Verses 19-21 tie the location of treasure to the direction of the heart.

options.text: Because owning any earthly possessions is sinful.
options.note: The issue is where the heart's treasure lies, not that possessions themselves are sinful.

options.text: Because heaven rewards those who first grow rich on earth.
options.note: Jesus contrasts the two treasures; he does not commend first storing up earthly wealth.

options.text: Because God has no interest in how we use money.
options.note: The whole passage shows God cares deeply how we treasure and use money.

quiz.q: What does Jesus mean by you cannot serve both God and money?

options.text: Money is a rival master; the heart cannot give undivided devotion to both it and God.
options.note: Verse 24 presents money as a competing lord demanding the allegiance owed to God.

options.text: It is impossible to be both wealthy and a believer.
options.note: The point is undivided allegiance, not that wealth and faith cannot coexist; many faithful people had means.

options.text: We should refuse to earn or handle money at all.
options.note: Jesus addresses the heart's master, not the mere handling of money.

options.text: God and money can be served equally with balance.
options.note: Jesus explicitly denies this; no one can serve two masters.

quiz.q: What is the remedy Jesus gives for anxiety?

options.text: Trust the Father who feeds the birds and clothes the lilies, and seek first His kingdom.
options.note: Verses 25-34 ground freedom from worry in the Father's care and the priority of His kingdom.

options.text: Work harder so you never lack food or clothing.
options.note: Jesus does not commend anxious striving; He points to trust in the Father, not self-reliance.

options.text: Ignore all practical needs as unspiritual.
options.note: He acknowledges real needs, the Father knows you need them, but calls for trust, not neglect.

options.text: Accept that God is indifferent to your daily needs.
options.note: The opposite; the Father knows and provides, so worry is unwarranted.

questions: Jesus says the Father sees in secret. How would living for an audience of One, rather than for people's approval, change the way you serve, give, or pray?
The Lord's Prayer begins with God's name, kingdom, and will before our needs. How might reordering your prayers this way reshape what you ask for?
Jesus links being forgiven with forgiving others. Is there someone you are refusing to forgive, and how does the mercy you have received in Christ move you toward them?
Where your treasure is, your heart will be also. What does the way you spend your money and time reveal about what you truly treasure?
Jesus calls anxious disciples you of little faith, then points to a caring Father. What worry is dominating you right now, and what would it look like to seek first the kingdom and trust Him with it?

translationNotes.note: Daily renders the rare word epiousios, most likely meaning the bread needed for the coming day, a call to daily dependence on the Father.
Deliver us from the evil one may also read from evil; some later manuscripts add the doxology, For Yours is the kingdom and the power and the glory, forever. Amen, noted in the BSB footnote.
Money renders mammon, an Aramaic term for wealth, here pictured as a rival master competing with God for the heart.
